clue.text: High Barnet as American might call it

definitions.text: High Barnet as American might call it

blocks.note: surface reading: a lofty district of north London, the town of High Barnet
setter's reading: Barnet is slang for hair, so a tall strip of hair, under its US name

explanation.surface: A visitor from the States renaming a north London suburb.
explanation.walkthrough: High Barnet is a real place at the end of a London Underground line, but 'barnet' is Cockney rhyming slang for hair (Barnet Fair). The British call the tall central crest a mohican; Americans use the other tribe's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Americans name the upright central stripe of shaved-sided hair after a Native American people, where Britons say mohican.

clue.text: Day ultimately spent on wine and port

indicators.note: ultimately means at the very end, so only the closing letter of the next word counts

blocks.note: the usual short form of Monday
its final letter
rosé is a pink wine; 'on' just places it after the others

explanation.surface: A whole day frittered away drinking wine and port.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Port' looks like more drink in the surface, but it is the definition: a harbour town on the east coast of Scotland, in Angus.
explanation.definitionFit: Montrose is a Scottish harbour town on the North Sea coast, so it is a seaport by example.

clue.text: I’m exasperated about nasty old lady

indicators.note: about can mean turned around, so the letters face the other way

blocks.note: an exclamation of irritation, as if the speaker is exasperated

explanation.surface: Someone at the end of their tether over a horrible elderly woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I'm exasperated' stands for the cry GAH! that such a person would utter; turned around, it gives HAG.
explanation.definitionFit: A hag is an insulting word for an ugly or unpleasant elderly woman, a crone or witch.

clue.text: A barrel containing heaven-sent Adam’s ale?

definitions.text: A barrel containing heaven-sent Adam’s ale?

blocks.clueFragment: A barrel containing heaven-sent Adam’s ale?
blocks.note: surface reading: a cask of some divine brew from the Garden of Eden
setter's reading: Adam's ale is an old joke name for plain drinking water, and what falls from heaven is rain

explanation.surface: A cask of the first man's beer, delivered from above.
explanation.walkthrough: Adam's ale is a jokey old phrase for water, since Adam had nothing else to drink; 'heaven-sent' means it fell as rain. A butt is also an old word for a large cask.
explanation.definitionFit: Gardeners keep a large barrel under a drainpipe to collect rainfall from the roof for watering plants.

clue.text: Ran out of kit at a sporting event

definitions.text: Ran out of kit at a sporting event

blocks.note: surface reading: a team or shop exhausted its supply of sports gear

blocks.clueFragment: Ran out of kit at a sporting event
blocks.note: setter's reading: dashed across the pitch with no clothes on

explanation.surface: A club's kit supply runs dry on match day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ran out of' reads as 'exhausted the supply of', but it means 'ran, being out of', that is, ran without any kit on: the famous naked dash across a pitch.
explanation.definitionFit: To streak is to run naked through a public place, classically across the field during a football or cricket match.

clue.text: Happily, her malt is what can give winger a lift

definitions.text: what can give winger a lift

indicators.note: doing something happily suggests a carefree jumble, so the letters are tossed into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A woman's whisky is the thing that cheers up a footballer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Winger' suggests a football wide player cheered by a drink, but here it is anything with wings, such as a bird or glider.
explanation.definitionFit: A rising column of warm air lifts soaring birds and gliders, so it raises a flying creature.

clue.text: Eusebio’s header fired up final for George Best

indicators.note: a header is what goes at the top, so only the opening letter is kept
the final of something is its end, so only the closing letter is kept

blocks.note: the first letter of the name
lit means set alight
the final letter

explanation.surface: The Portuguese striker Eusebio scores with his head in a final against Manchester United's George Best.
explanation.walkthrough: The footballing words all do letter work: 'header' and 'final' pick out letters, and Best is not the Northern Irish player but the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The elite are the top group, the finest or most select people, so the word serves as the best.

clue.text: Drunk quickly given the cold shoulder?

blocks.note: first meaning: a drink downed in one go
second meaning: turned down or rebuffed

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a drunk person being snubbed; the two halves are separate senses of one phrasal verb.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang a drink is knocked back when swallowed fast, and a person is knocked back when their approach is rejected.

clue.text: Tyrant has no power over explorer

indicators.note: having none of something means it is missing, so that letter is taken away

blocks.note: a despot is an absolute ruler
P is the standard abbreviation for power
O is the cricket scorer's abbreviation for an over

explanation.surface: A dictator is left powerless over an adventurer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over' looks like a preposition but is the cricket abbreviation O, added after DESOT.
explanation.definitionFit: Hernando de Soto was a sixteenth-century Spanish conquistador who led the first European expedition across the American south-east.

clue.text: Jack up part of car that’s stuck on the road

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading from the bottom, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: jack and tar are both old words for a sailor
a cam is a rotating part in an engine

explanation.surface: Raising a broken-down car with a jack at the roadside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jack up' looks like the phrase for raising a car, but Jack is the sailor and 'up' reverses the next part.
explanation.definitionFit: Tarmac is the bitumen-and-stone surfacing laid down and bonded onto roadways.

clue.text: Horseman skipping initial horse trial

indicators.note: skipping the start means jumping over the opening letter, so it is dropped

blocks.note: a knight is a mounted soldier
a mare is a female horse

explanation.surface: A rider misses the first event of an equestrian competition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Horse trial' reads as an equestrian event, but trial alone is the definition, an ordeal; the silent K is the initial dropped.
explanation.definitionFit: A nightmare in its figurative sense is a dreadful, harrowing experience, an ordeal like a trial.

clue.text: One’s to arrest Tory sex symbols

indicators.note: to arrest is to seize and hold, so one piece takes another into custody inside it

blocks.note: one is I, with the S of the possessive kept
Con is the short form of Conservative

explanation.surface: Someone means to arrest a Conservative MP in a sex scandal.
explanation.walkthrough: Tory is the everyday name for a member of Britain's Conservative Party, abbreviated Con.
explanation.definitionFit: Glamorous stars admired as emblems of sexual attraction are often called icons, a celebrity sense of the word.

clue.text: East German radical opens liquor stand

indicators.note: whatever opens something comes at the front, fixing the order of the parts

blocks.note: R is an abbreviation for radical
Ost is the German word for east
rum is a spirit

explanation.surface: A militant from the old GDR launches a bar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'East German' looks like a citizen of the former GDR, but it means the German word for east.
explanation.definitionFit: A rostrum is a raised platform a speaker or conductor stands on, so it is a stand or dais.

clue.text: Seats held and carried by Labour?

definitions.text: Seats held and carried by Labour?

blocks.clueFragment: Seats held and carried by Labour?
blocks.note: surface reading: parliamentary constituencies retained and won by the Labour Party
setter's reading: seats lifted up and borne along by hired workers

explanation.surface: An election night report on the constituencies the Labour Party kept.
explanation.walkthrough: Labour is Britain's main left-wing party, and 'seats held and carried' sounds like votes; the capital L disguises plain manual labour, the porters who carried these.
explanation.definitionFit: These enclosed chairs on poles were carried through the streets by two porters, a passenger seat moved by human muscle.

clue.text: Spooner’s declared Starmer “lacklustre beast”.

indicators.note: Dr Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of neighbouring words, so his speech tells you to do the same

blocks.note: the Labour leader's first name; it takes the opening sound of the other word
matt means dull, not shiny; it takes the opening sound of the other word

explanation.surface: Dr Spooner dismisses the Prime Minister as a dull animal.
explanation.walkthrough: Keir Starmer became the UK's Labour Prime Minister in 2024. KEIR MATT with the K and M sounds swapped gives MEER KAT.
explanation.definitionFit: A meerkat is a small southern African mongoose, an animal, so any creature word like beast fits.

clue.text: I hold mid-course at sea for salt

indicators.note: being at sea means confused and lost, so the letters are thrown into disorder

blocks.note: taken as written, ignoring the hyphen

explanation.surface: A sailor keeps a steady heading halfway through a voyage, seeking salt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At sea' fits the nautical surface so well that it hides its job as the signal to rearrange the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Common table seasoning is chemically the compound NaCl, which is the scientific name for ordinary salt.

clue.text: Errors I’ve rectified in VAT

indicators.note: to rectify is to put right by rearranging, so the letters are fixed into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, ignoring the apostrophe

explanation.surface: An accountant fixes mistakes in a value added tax return.
explanation.walkthrough: VAT in capitals reads as value added tax, Britain's sales tax; the capitals disguise an ordinary vat, a big tank for liquid.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words name a large container or tank in which liquid is stored, so a reservoir is a kind of vat.

clue.text: Certain to tuck into boozy drink? Steady!

indicators.note: to tuck into something is to slip inside it, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: mead is an alcoholic drink of fermented honey
sure means certain

explanation.surface: Someone about to tuck into a strong drink is told to take it easy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Steady!' sounds like a warning to a drinker, but it is an adjective here, meaning even and deliberate.
explanation.definitionFit: A measured pace or tone is slow, regular and controlled, which is what steady describes.

clue.text: IM isn’t seen sat playing with a GM

indicators.note: pieces that are playing move around freely, so the letters are reshuffled

blocks.note: taken as written, ignoring the apostrophe
taken as written

explanation.surface: A chess International Master hides from view while sitting down to play a Grandmaster.
explanation.walkthrough: IM and GM look like chess titles, International Master and Grandmaster; IM is really the abbreviation being defined, and GM is just two letters of fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: IM is the standard abbreviation for a text sent in real time over an online chat service.

clue.text: Indian greeting celebrity holding short drink

indicators.note: holding something means keeping it within, so one piece goes inside another
short means cut off, so the last letter is lopped away

blocks.note: a big name is a famous person
Asti is a sparkling Italian wine

explanation.surface: A famous Indian figure greets someone while holding a small glass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Short drink' suggests a shot of spirits, but 'short' trims the I from the end of the wine.
explanation.definitionFit: Namaste is the traditional Hindu salutation, said with palms pressed together and a slight bow.

clue.text: Flash bag holding one’s artwork

indicators.note: holding something means keeping it within, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: a mo is a moment, as is a flash
a sac is a bag-like pouch
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A showy handbag containing a work of art.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flash' reads as an adjective meaning showy, but it is a noun: an instant, a mo. The 's after one stands for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: A mosaic is a picture or pattern made by setting small pieces of coloured stone or glass, a decorative artwork.

clue.text: Top team occasionally ignored linesman

indicators.note: ignoring every other letter means skipping some at regular intervals, so only alternate letters are kept

blocks.note: the first and third letters
a poet writes lines of verse, so is a lines-man

explanation.surface: A leading football side overlooked the assistant referee's flag.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Linesman' suggests the official running the touchline, but it is a man of lines, a poet. Top is the garment, not 'best'.
explanation.definitionFit: A tabard is a sleeveless tunic or overgarment, so it is a top in the clothing sense.

clue.text: What He is mostly limiting?

indicators.note: to limit is to set bounds around, so the outer words enclose the letters we want

blocks.note: the letters run across these words

explanation.surface: A question about what restricts God, the capital-H He.
explanation.walkthrough: The run starts inside 'What' and ends inside 'mostly'. Read as a whole, the clue also describes the answer: a belief that curbs the role of the capitalised He, God.
explanation.definitionFit: Disbelief in any deity denies God's existence altogether, so it is the ultimate restriction on the divine.

clue.text: Offender letting slip small secret

indicators.note: letting something slip means losing hold of it, so that letter falls away

blocks.note: a sinner is one who offends against moral law
S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing sizes

explanation.surface: A criminal accidentally reveals a minor confidence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Letting slip' suggests blurting out a secret, but it means dropping a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Inner feelings or thoughts are private and hidden from others, so the adjective works as a synonym for secret.

clue.text: Clearly Men at Work had no part in these hits

definitions.text: Clearly Men at Work had no part in these

blocks.clueFragment: Clearly Men at Work had no part in these
blocks.note: first meaning: walkouts, when workers down tools, so nobody is at work
second meaning: blows or punches

explanation.walkthrough: Men at Work were an Australian band with chart hits in the 1980s, so the clue seems to be about music; but men on a walkout are by definition not at work.
explanation.definitionFit: Industrial stoppages are walkouts by employees, and blows landed on someone are hits; one word covers both senses.

clue.text: Strange story appearing in article

indicators.note: something appearing in another shows up inside it, so one piece sits within the other

blocks.note: an is the indefinite article
a story can be an untruth, a lie

explanation.surface: An odd tale is printed in a newspaper feature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Article' suggests a news piece, but it is the grammatical article.
explanation.definitionFit: Alien as an adjective means unfamiliar or foreign, belonging elsewhere, which is close to strange.

clue.text: How’s rep dancing along with In the Navy?

indicators.note: dancing feet move about in all directions, so the letters are moved around

blocks.note: taken as written, ignoring the apostrophe
taken as written

explanation.surface: A reviewer asks how a dance troupe got on with the Village People's disco hit In the Navy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the Navy' looks like a song title, but In belongs with the fodder and 'the Navy' is the definition. The question mark flags a definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: A navy possesses a fleet of warships, so it is one example of an organisation that owns vessels.

clue.text: Little crash … pot kicked over?

indicators.note: something kicked over is upended, so the letters are turned the other way

blocks.note: a pan is a cooking pot

explanation.surface: A minor kitchen accident when a pot gets knocked over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crash' suggests a collision, but in slang to crash is to fall asleep, so a little crash is a short sleep.
explanation.definitionFit: A nap is a brief doze, and crashing out is informal for going to sleep, so a small one is a snooze.

clue.text: Diplomatic insult island caught on wiretap

indicators.note: a wiretap picks up what is heard, so the word is taken by its sound rather than its spelling

blocks.note: dis is slang for disrespect or insult
Crete is the large Greek island

explanation.surface: An ambassador's slur about an island is recorded by phone tapping.
explanation.walkthrough: DIS + CRETE gives DISCRETE (separate), which sounds the same as the answer; the spelling heard is the one meaning tactful.
explanation.definitionFit: Being discreet means careful and tactful about what one says, the quality of a good diplomat.

clue.text: In a heartless way, seized and released grouse

indicators.note: without a heart means the centre is missing, so the middle letter goes

blocks.note: gripped means held tightly

explanation.surface: A gamebird is cruelly caught and then set free.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grouse' looks like the gamebird, but here it is a complaint; releasing one means voicing a moan.
explanation.definitionFit: To gripe is to complain, and a grouse is a grumble, so letting one out is griping.
